cards.front: In Java, when the left operand of && is false, is the right operand evaluated?
cards.extra: false && anything is always false, so Java never evaluates the right side. That is what makes guard clauses safe: a null check, a zero check, or an expensive call on the right runs only when the left passes.
cards.example:
int divisor = 0;
if (divisor != 0 && (10 / divisor > 2)) {
    System.out.println("Result is greater than 2");
}
// no ArithmeticException: 10 / divisor is never evaluated

cards.front: In Java, when the left operand of || is true, is the right operand evaluated?
cards.extra: true || anything is always true. Use it to bail out before a risky or expensive right-hand check, such as reading scores[index] after an index-validity test.
cards.example:
int index = -1;
int[] scores = {10, 20, 30};
if (index < 0 || scores[index] == 10) {
    System.out.println("Invalid index or score is 10");
}
// no ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: scores[index] is never evaluated

cards.front: In Java's ternary ?:, are both branches evaluated?
cards.back: No — only the branch matching the condition; the other is never evaluated.
cards.extra: Java evaluates the condition first, then executes just the selected branch. Side effects in the skipped branch do not happen — unlike arguments to a method call, which are all evaluated eagerly.
cards.example:
int a = 5, b = 5;
int result = (a == 5) ? ++a : ++b;
// result = 6, a = 6, b = 5  (++b never ran)
